posts.title: Amelia Island Museum of History in Fernandina Beach, Florida
posts.excerpt:
The Amelia Island Museum of History invites guests to step back in time and experience 4,000 years of rich regional history. posts.excerpt: Astronomers have determined that VVV CL001, a metal-poor globular cluster near the center of the Milky Way, is about 13.4 billion years old, making it one of the oldest known star clusters in our galaxy. The paper, outlining the methodology for estimating its age and distance, was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 20. It has been accepted for publication by Astronomy & Astrophysics.

posts.title: Someone Else on the Mountain: The Unseen Companions of Climbers and Explorers
posts.excerpt: Descending through mist on Ben Macdui, Norman Collie began to hear footsteps behind him. Every few steps he took were followed by a heavier crunch, as though another walker were covering the same ground with a much longer stride. He could see nobody. He listened again, tried to dismiss what he was hearing, and continued down the mountain. The sounds continued too. Eventually, the experienced mountaineer became so frightened that he fled, stumbling among the boulders for miles towards Rothiemurchus Forest.

posts.title: This oddball reflective lava world is challenging to understand
posts.excerpt: Among Kepler and TESS's many surprising exoplanet discoveries are the ultra-short-period (USP) planets. These planets move very quickly and complete an orbit in less than 24 hours. Ancient astronomers thought that Mercury was so fast—it goes around the sun every 88 days—that they named it after the Roman god Mercury, who was the fast-traveling messenger of the gods. They couldn't have known how sluggish Mercury is compared to the USPs.

posts.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
posts.excerpt: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit.

posts.title: St. John's Episcopal Church in Franklin, Pennsylvania
posts.excerpt:
Nestled on a quiet back street in the once-booming oil town of Franklin, PA, sits St. John's Episcopal Church. While the exterior is pleasing and well-maintained, the true treasures are discovered once you pass through the large wood-and-iron doors.  
 Every window at St. John's was created by the studios of Louis Comfort Tiffany! Furthermore, St. John's is one of only seven remaining churches with a complete collection of Tiffany windows.  
 The main sanctuary houses a Rose Window (the 3rd largest ever created by Tiffany Studios) as well as a series of triptychs depicting the life of Christ.

posts.title: Different transcription systems shape chromatin behavior in distinct nuclear regions
posts.excerpt: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which are further organized into chromatin. Chromatin has traditionally been divided into transcriptionally active euchromatin and relatively inactive heterochromatin. However, chromatin is not a fixed structure. Nucleosomes continuously move within the nucleus, and this motion is closely related to the physical organization and function of the genome.

posts.title: Customizable nanoparticles show potential for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
posts.excerpt: A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines. The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.

posts.title: Lab-aged microplastics enable tests of interactions with contaminants
posts.excerpt: A newly published study advances our knowledge of how microplastics may age in the environment and whether they stick to other contaminants as they do so. Microplastics (MPs) are tiny plastic pieces that measure less than 5 millimeters (about 0.2 inches) in length. The study looked at the aging of MPs made of three common polymer chemicals—polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate and polypropylene—to see if they changed as they aged and how that affected nearby contaminants.

posts.excerpt: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in which electrons can move with high mobility, making it promising for high-speed electronic components. posts.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
posts.excerpt: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. posts.title: Rainfall can travel from mountain slopes to rivers far faster than expected in mountain catchments
posts.excerpt: Researchers at University of Tsukuba have found that river responses to rainfall can reach rivers and appear as runoff much more rapidly than previously assumed in mountainous regions. Through continuous monitoring of precipitation and river water levels, they documented rapid rainfall-related responses not only in moderate-relief catchments but also in high-relief catchments with mountain slopes exceeding 500 m in length. The findings provide new insights into runoff generation and flood development in mountainous regions. The paper is published in the Journal of Hydrology.

posts.excerpt: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. posts.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
posts.excerpt: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

posts.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
posts.excerpt: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

posts.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
posts.excerpt: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun.  This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year.   Continue
